chief_complaint: progressive fatigue and elevated creatinine on routine lab
hpi_details: A 23-year-old male with no prior diagnosis of diabetes or hypertension presents after an elevated creatinine was found on routine bloodwork for a pre-employment physical. He reports feeling mildly more fatigued than usual over the past few months but otherwise feels well, denying edema, foamy urine, or gross hematuria.
ideas: He thinks his elevated kidney level is simply from pushing himself too hard during heavy weightlifting workouts and consuming protein shakes.
concerns: He is worried that this abnormal test result will disqualify him from passing his medical screening and cause his employer to revoke his job offer.
expectations: He hopes to repeat the blood test after hydrating and resting so the doctor can sign his employment clearance form today.

available_results.note: This is the newly discovered abnormal result prompting the encounter; chronicity has not yet been established.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Kidney Disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management includes optimizing blood pressure control and starting an ACEi/ARB for proteinuria, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive fatigue and elevated creatinine on routine lab

Key HPI features: A 23-year-old male with no prior diagnosis of diabetes or hypertension presents after an elevated creatinine was found on routine bloodwork for a pre-employment physical. He reports feeling mildly more fatigued than usual over the past few months but otherwise feels well, denying edema, foamy urine, or gross hematuria.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 76, afebrile, BMI 27. No peripheral edema, no pallor. Labs: Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2, urinalysis with 1+ protein, no hematuria. Repeat creatinine one week later remains elevated (2.0 mg/dL), confirming the abnormality is real rather than a transient laboratory error; chronicity is NOT yet established, because CKD requires kidney damage or reduced GFR persisting for at least 3 months, so prior records and repeat testing at 3 months are needed to separate CKD from acute kidney disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Kidney Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute kidney injury without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Significant swelling, breathlessness, or confusion — suggests advanced disease.
management_principles: Optimize blood pressure control and start an ACEi/ARB for proteinuria
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Kidney Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 23M with no prior diagnosis of diabetes or hypertension presents after an elevated creatinine was found on routine bloodwork for a pre-employment physical. He reports feeling mildly more fatigued than usual over the past few months but otherwise feels well, denying edema, foamy urine, or gross hematuria.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 76, afebrile, BMI 27. No peripheral edema, no pallor. Labs: Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2, urinalysis with 1+ protein, no hematuria. Repeat creatinine one week later remains elevated (2.0 mg/dL), confirming the abnormality is real rather than a transient laboratory error; chronicity is NOT yet established, because CKD requires kidney damage or reduced GFR persisting for at least 3 months, so prior records and repeat testing at 3 months are needed to separate CKD from acute kidney disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Elevated creatinine requires evaluation; chronic kidney disease is defined by persistent kidney abnormality for at least 3 months and cannot be confirmed from a single routine laboratory result.
reference_soap.plan: Repeat kidney-function testing and obtain urinalysis/urine albumin-creatinine ratio to distinguish acute kidney injury from chronic kidney disease and establish chronicity. Optimize blood pressure control and use ACE inhibitor/ARB for albuminuria when indicated, with creatinine and potassium monitoring. Refer promptly for significant proteinuria, rapidly changing kidney function, or advanced disease.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Chronic Kidney Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Chronic Kidney Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: Optimize blood pressure control, ACEi/ARB for proteinuria

teaching.one_liner: Progressive, often silent, decline in kidney function usually from long-standing hypertension or diabetes causing glomerular injury.
red_flags: Significant swelling, breathlessness, or confusion — suggests advanced disease

must_ask.say: How long have you had diabetes or high blood pressure?
Was this found on a routine blood test?
Any changes in your urine — foaminess or color?

history.answer: I came in because they told me my kidney function number was high on my pre-employment health screening, and I've also been feeling more tired lately.
I did a pre-employment blood test about two weeks ago, and the clinic called to tell me that my kidney marker was higher than normal.
I had a health checkup four years ago before entering college, and all my blood and urine tests were completely normal back then.
I fasted for twelve hours overnight, drank plenty of water, and didn't have any coffee, tobacco, or heavy exercise before the test.
I have never checked my blood pressure or blood sugar at home because I didn't think I had any health problems.
I've been feeling unusually tired and sluggish over the past couple of months, but I haven't had headaches, extreme thirst, or frequent urination.
I haven't had any chest pain, shortness of breath, blurred vision, or weakness or numbness on either side.
My urine looks clear yellow without any blood or foam, and I don't have any pain in my sides or lower back.
I haven't noticed any swelling in my legs, ankles, or around my eyes, and my weight has stayed the same.
No fevers, night sweats, unexpected weight loss, swollen glands, or coughing up blood at all.
I don't have any pain or burning when I pee, no urinary hesitancy, and I haven't had prostate trouble, urinary infections, or recent bike rides.
I haven't had muscle cramps, severe weakness, heart racing, excessive sweating, or loud snoring at night.
I don't take pain medications like ibuprofen, steroid pills, decongestants, or any herbal supplements.
I eat regular home-cooked meals with occasional takeout, and I try to go for light jogs on the weekend.
I have never broken any bones, haven't gotten shorter, and have never taken steroid medications.
I've never had tuberculosis, haven't been around anyone sick with it, and have no immune system disorders.
I thought the high kidney number was just because I've been working out really heavy at the gym and drinking high-protein shakes lately.
I'm really worried that this test result is going to disqualify me and make the company pull back my job offer.
I was hoping we could just re-run the blood test after I drink some water so you can sign off on my employment clearance form today.
I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, kidney trouble, or any other medical conditions.
I've never had any operations and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I'm not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or vitamins right now.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else that I know of.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes in my life.
I only drink socially, usually just one or two beers once or twice a month with friends.
I recently graduated from university, live with my parents, and I'm preparing to start an office job.
No one in my family has kidney disease, early heart attacks, stroke, high blood pressure, or diabetes.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, pulse 76 beats per minute, afebrile, respirations 14 breaths per minute, BMI 27 kg/m2.
Well-nourished young male in no acute distress; slightly overweight.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and texture, with no nodules, tenderness, or bruits.
Regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Breath sounds are clear and equal bilaterally without crackles or wheezes.
Normoactive bowel sounds; no abdominal aorta or renal artery bruits heard.
Abdomen is soft and non-tender; no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or abnormal masses.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
Radial, femoral, and dorsalis pedis pulses are intact, 2+, and symmetric bilaterally.
Normal spinal curvature without kyphosis; no tenderness along the thoracic or lumbar spine.
No pretibial or pedal pitting edema on either lower extremity.
Normal sphincter tone; prostate is smooth, non-tender, and normal in size without nodules.
